utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone, including those in the field office of Sarajevo. Could we begin by taking the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Joanna Korner assisted this morning by Jasmina Bosnjakovic as Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for the Defence of Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Ivana Batista.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Judge Peric. Can you still hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I invite Mr. -- before I invite Mr. Cvijetic to resume his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us resume. To avoid wasting time, can we please have P120 on the screen. That is an exhibit that's under tab 23 in your binder. Mr. Peric, I hope you have the document in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm a thing that shouldn't be contentious, namely that this is the federal law on criminal proceeding that was applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the relevant period, and for all practical purposes it was in use until 2000 -- in the year 2000 when the reform of the legal system in Bosnia had taken place. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will also agree that, in essence, this is the basic piece of regulation which shows the rights and the duties, as well as the roles of all the subjects that take part in a criminal proceeding. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Registrar to put page 14 in the English version on the screen, and in the B/C/S version it's page 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I'm interested in Article 45.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's see if we can interpret this article. This is an article where basic rights and duties of the public prosecutors are determined in the processing and criminal prosecution of perpetrators of crimes. Therefore, under (1), we can see that it is the basic right and basic duty of the public prosecutor, the prosecution of perpetrators of criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As it is stated in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In item number (2), we see elaboration of legal measures that -- or steps that are to be taken to achieve this goal. And then under Roman I, we can see that the public prosecutor takes necessary steps to discover criminal acts and to find the perpetrators and to guide preliminary criminal proceedings. Can you see that text?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Under Roman II, it's the public prosecutor, you, who requests for an investigation to be conducted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Under Roman III, it is the prosecutor who brings the indictment before the competent court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing contentious there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And under IV, you're entitled do appeal against court decisions that have not come into effect.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Item number (3), you have the right to take other steps specified by the law. Mr. Peric, the Chamber, this Chamber here, holds a view that I believe; namely, that one need not interpret something that is obvious in itself, and I believe this text is. However, my question to you is: At which stage, according to you, the criminal proceeding starts, and when does an official processing of a crime start, the processing of the perpetrator as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By starting the investigation, by launching the criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, your request to the investigative judge to launch an investigation is the start of a criminal proceeding; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Criminal proceeding may start without investigation as well, if you decide to [indiscernible] the indictment without a previous investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or a bill of indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all we wanted to do with this provision. Now, can we move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, it's page 42 and then 43. We'll be needing both pages. In the B/C/S version, it's page 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, for you, we're looking for Article 148. Have you located it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will not be reading the article. I would just like to ask you whether we agree on something. So the criminal report to the prosecutor, i.e., to you, can be submitted by all the -- all those mentioned in Article 148, as well as in 149?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, we already have that article on the screen; in the B/C/S version, I would like to ask to move to the following page. Can we please have the following page in B/C/S version so that Article 149 would be displayed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you see Article 149?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So all those enumerated here, and I would like to stress any citizen, can make a criminal report to you, if they have information that a crime has been committed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In Article 150 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask to go to the following page in B/C/S version, because that's where the Article 150 is. In the English version, we already have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, could you -- if I might interrupt you briefly, could you assist me, please, so that I may follow the line of questions that you're pursuing. Assuming that at the end of the present exercise in which you were engaged, the Chamber, the witness, and yourself are all agreed as to what the effect and meaning of these laws -- of -- of the fundamental law is, where would that place us, in terms of the purpose for which this witness has been called? If I understand where you're heading in that direction, then perhaps I would be in a better position to follow where we are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will explain. Before I start putting specific questions regarding the cases that this prosecutor had been dealing with in Teslic, the cases that he talked about yesterday, I must remind him of the provisions and the regulations and to remind him what his duties and rights were, according to such regulations. We will not stay on an academic level so to speak. There will be practical results. We will demonstrate to the Trial Chamber what is it that I want to stress. I will just quickly go through this set of regulations and then I'll start putting specific questions related to the implementation of the regulation, in relation to his work in Teslic. Furthermore, you will have had time go through his statement, you will see the difference in the interpretation of the regulation between the statement and what's stated in it and the regulations itself. I will quickly go through the regulations, and then we'll go to the specifics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I note you used the word "quickly" twice. We hold you to that, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, if I may, do have you to remind the witness of his duties? Is that your role?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not only that. I thought I already explained why I do need to go through the regulations here. May I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, as part of the submitting of the criminal report, you as the prosecutor could have also had personal information that a crime has been committed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a hypothetical possibility. However, I was, in practice, probably the last one who would have found out about a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But yesterday you discussed a situation in which you had personal information about some crimes that had been committed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was much after the actual commission of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For the time being, let's stay at this level. So would you agree with me that the prosecutor also can have personal information about the commission of a crime, and after having received such information, he can launch certain measures and steps. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I agree with you. I'm not questioning any of the provisions, and I'm familiar with them. Maybe if you'd start putting specific questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in a situation as a public prosecutor that a citizen comes to you and verbally tells you that a crime was committed and that he or she wants a proceeding to be launched against the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've been a prosecutor for three years; I've never been in such a situation. Citizens normally report crimes to the police. And never ever has any citizen come to me to report a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the law provides for that possibility, namely, to come to you and put into record, as we put it, their criminal report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The law contains main provisions that do not have practical use or did not have practical use.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask to go page -- to -- to page 131 in B/C/S. It's page 46 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I'm interested in Articles 157 and 158. Have you found them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that, under the system at the time, the investigation is conducted by the investigative judge, based on a request by the public prosecutor? We can see that in these two articles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us now move to the last provision I intend to show you. We will not go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 76 in the English version; page 205 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It is Article 261. Sorry, I failed to mention it before. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It is stated here that the criminal proceeding can be conducted only based on an indictment issued by the public prosecutors and on -- in some cases the victim as the prosecutor. We understand each other, don't we?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Peric, let me summarise the position of the Defence, in relation to implementation of the provisions here. The prosecution of the perpetrators and their processing before the judicial organs at the time was exclusively part of the authorities of the public prosecutor; and then further processing would be under the authority of the relevant court.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecution, yes; but preparation and collection of evidence was something that was to be done by the police. One must make a distinction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me put a question to you. All the steps that precede the initiating of the criminal proceedings is not part of the criminal proceedings and falls under the so-called preliminary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was called was pre-criminal proceedings in our language, but we can, in a way, treat it as part of the criminal proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: From the moment when a criminal prosecution starts before judicial organs, this prosecution is within the exclusive competence of the judicial bodies, and they are independent in their work in which nobody may interfere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That follows from the laws and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The role of the police ceases at the moment when a criminal prosecution starts before judicial bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now a practical issue. When you start an investigation against several persons, and in the course of that investigation the investigating judge establishes that apart from the persons reported there are other persons responsible for the crime, you may put in an application to expand the investigation to include them as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will put to you the position of this Defence concerning the role and the tasks of the police in the identification and apprehension of perpetrators and the collection of evidence. You will agree with me that the Ministry of Interior is an organ of state administration and that identification and apprehension of perpetrators is not their only job and responsibility, because, as an organ of state administration, they deal with a number of other affairs that are not related to the apprehension of perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then we will not open the Law on Internal Affairs because that is written in Article 15 of that law. I believe you even mentioned it yesterday. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, before I desist from looking into military regulations, and you were shown the relevant law by Mrs. Korner yesterday, I would like honest answer from you. It was my impression yesterday that you don't feel well-prepared enough to speak as an expert about the jurisdiction of military courts, the organisation of their work and their operation, in terms of applying legislation and in practice in 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not really deal much with that side of the legislation. I know the basics about their jurisdiction. I tried to explain that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We are also familiar with the basics. For other matters, we will find an expert. I just want to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we call up 1D170. Tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the latter part of the decision, proclaiming an imminent threat of war and a general mobilisation of the entire territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as stated in the heading. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 16 of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was proclaimed? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it. I did not see this decision. But I believe it was implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You've just anticipated my question. I was about to ask you if you knew about its application, so thank you. Since you did not know about this decision, I'll just ask you a general question. With the proclamation of an imminent threat of war and the general public mobilisation, all military age, able-bodied men practically became conscripts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a fair inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This fact had a significant impact on the expansion of the jurisdiction of military courts because, with this, roughly 95 per cent of the estimated number of perpetrators and offenders passed to the jurisdiction of military authorities and military courts. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you can make that conclusion. I don't think this expanded their jurisdiction as stipulated by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At any rate, even if we link this with the law, all these persons would pass to the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Only when they are integrated into military units can they become -- can they pass under the authority of military authorities and courts. This decision itself does not place them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I mean a situation when they are actually mobilised, and this decision provides for it. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But from the proclamation until they are displaced at the disposal of military units there is a span of time. It's not automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We don't quite agree on this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I'm not an expert in this field either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let us see if we can make anything out of this legislation. Yesterday, in response to questions by Ms. Korner, you said that in the process of prosecuting the group known as Mices, in the course of the investigation and based on some statements of suspects, you began to suspect that some additional persons should also be investigated that were not covered by the investigation currently.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I intended to expand my investigation after leading the evidence I had originally envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Why did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because exhumations were required. And after wrapping up all the evidence only could I expand the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, exhumation could hardly have been the reason why you failed to prosecute this Mr. Savic from Doboj. You were able to prosecute him even without exhumations.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without exhumations, I did not have the possibility to expand the investigation; and without expanding it, I was not able to complete it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you personally had suspicions and information that certain crimes had been committed and that the identity of the perpetrators was even known, but that information had not reached you as the prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the prosecutor's office, you handled -- rather, you kept several records?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The main log-book was the so-called KT log-book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Into that log-book, information was logged on identified perpetrators, and records were made of all the steps made by the prosecutor to prosecute that person.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That log-book contained information exclusively about known, identified perpetrators and all the steps taken during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Entries were also made as to whether the person was remanded in custody, whether a judgement was made, and whether you appealed against that judgement.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also kept a log-book, KTN, which logged information relating to unidentified perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The moment a perpetrator is identified, you would transfer that information to the KT log-book?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also kept a KTM log-book, entering information about perpetrators who are minors, under 18; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also had a KTA log-book. KTA. Where you would log all the other documents, documents issued by you, and your correspondence with other authorities that did not belong in any of the other log-books. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you specifically: If you would find out that in the territory of the Teslic municipality a crime had been committed and that it was known even who the perpetrator was but you did not receive that information officially, you had the power, as prosecutor, to ask the police to collect the necessary information; and if you knew who the perpetrator was, you were even authorised to start an investigation. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The prosecutor had those powers. But these powers were irrelevant, in practice. They had no practical value. I also knew one other thing, and I learned that from inspectors with whom I had close relations; namely, that the collegium of the police had a meeting each morning, deciding what would be prosecuted and what would not. And knowing that there were crimes that are not deliberately prosecuted, I wrote up a report in which I wrote exactly what that means and stating some recommendations to deal with this situation. So I did have to correspond with the police every time, but that was pointless. I did not want to do things that would not have a practical result. But I submitted that report to the Assembly where the chief of the public security station was represented and the chief of -- and the commander of the police. But that was the state of our judicial system and the security system in Teslic municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, you will agree with me that you skipped the legal channel which I indicated to you when reading the laws. And you are responsible for an omission here, because you should have left a trace of your actions as the law stipulates?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can take it as an omission, but it is not, de facto, an omission, because if I had done it, it would have had no meaning, no effect. And, finally, I talked to the people in the police and asked them to deal with all the cases. I knew they were aware of certain cases which they did not want to deal with. And it was pointless for me to correspond with the police. If I had written letters to them in every single case, that could have been interpreted in a different way, and I maybe would not have been sitting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you have at your disposal an investigating judge --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I was just indicating to Mr. Cvijetic that he is starting his question before we finished receiving information, and I wonder if there could be a slight gap between the answer and his asking the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you left no trace in terms of procedure before an investigating judge in the cases involving known perpetrators where you did not have to correspond with the police. You were able to start an investigation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me one case involving a known perpetrator which I failed to prosecute?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm citing your words. You said yesterday that there were cases where the perpetrators were known and the case never reached your desk. And I'm asking: If you were aware of such cases, why didn't you start an investigation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the police was aware of such cases with known perpetrators and failed to do anything and inform the prosecutor. I didn't say I knew about them. You must have misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your KTA log-book, is it the case that there are entries made by you to -- concerning cases where you intervened to the -- with the -- interceded with the republican public prosecutor and other authorities and cases like those you cite?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if -- if there is any evidence. There should be. I don't think I deal -- I dealt with that. I don't think I sent such reports to the republican prosecutor, apart from annual reports. You should look into the annual reports that I sent to the republic prosecutor and what exactly I wrote there. I cannot tell you now what exactly I put in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, the only authority above you were the law and the constitution; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you think you were unable to discharge your functions under the law and the constitution, why didn't you simply resign?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discharged my functions to the best of my ability, to the extent of my ability, and I did it, I believe, very conscientiously. And professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This post you occupied, in addition to rights and responsibilities, did it confer upon you certain privileges?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only privilege I enjoyed was that I was not called to the front line, to the army, if you can talk about privileges at the time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you believe it was a privilege that in those times of crisis you still received a regular salary?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's a privilege. In addition, I believe that, for a while, we didn't even receive pay. For more than a half -- than half a year, I believe, we received no pay at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I've read your statement given to the OTP, and you appear now to be very critical of the system and the authorities and their failure to act in that period. My question is: Weren't you a part of that system and those authorities? Because it was precisely that system and those authorities which placed you in a very important position which you occupied throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a broad sense, in a constitutional, legal sense, I was part of the authorities, but, in reality, I was not a part of local authorities. If you remember, I explained at the first meeting, when I was asked to become part of the Crisis Staff, I said I did not want to get involved with any Crisis Staff; I wanted to do my job professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you did accept an unlawful and illegal appointment to that position, and until the end of August, you continued in that position unlawfully.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can interpret in that way but it was a combination of circumstances. And I think is it far important that I accepted to do that job than the mere fact that it was done at the moment in a way which was not completely in line with the law. In certain situations, you are guided by practical purposes, and that was one of those times. I think you would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm asking you. Those authorities also had to improvise a lot of the way. They could not operate with perfection in 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my problem. I don't think I can agree it was necessary and indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's not a problem when others are concerned, but you accepted that measure of improvisation when you are concerned.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not accept improvisation just because it was about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You seem to be a legalist. You should be principled then.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not a matter of principle. I was the most experienced person at the time. I had ten years of experience as prosecutor and judge at the time. Nobody matched that experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that that begs the question of the legality of all the actions you took as a prosecutor at the time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will leave it to others to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move now to the issue of your termination of position. I think you discussed that issue for your statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also discussed some unofficial initiatives to relieve you of that duty. I think primarily there was one -- that the initiative was launched by the SDS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen the document which was the basis for the request for me being relieved of duty. It was shown to my by the state prosecutor. It was a letter to the main board of the SDS. There were several letters of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was also an initiative launched by almost all the workers and your colleagues from the judicial building. It was a petition asking for you to be relieved of duty. Do you know of that document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was in regard to the president of the court, not in regard to public prosecutor. I had only two employees, and neither of them asked for me to be relieved of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, these are unofficial, informal acts, and the position of this Defence in regard to such documents and newspaper articles is such that we do not consider them relevant evidence to be presented before this Tribunal. However, I intend to deal with the official reasons for your relief of duty, so those that were legally valid.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would love to hear the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I would like to have 1D03-3321 on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I have an objection to the way this is being dealt it, that it was suggested to Judge Peric that there was an initiative launched by the workers and colleagues from the judicial building, a petition for you asking to resign, and he says no. And then Mr. Cvijetic makes a statement: "These are unofficial, informal acts, and the position of this Defence in regard to such documents and newspaper articles is ... we do not consider them relevant evidence." Your Honours, if that's the case, then it's improper to put a suggestion based on such documents which he has not intended to put to the judge so he can deal with them. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I terribly apologise. Clients doesn't receive translation. So ... THE ACCUSED ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] I'm not hearing a translation of what Ms. Korner was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Zupljanin hear me now? No, apparently. Testing ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Keep on talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I can see Mr. Zupljanin shaking his head. I'm just wondering whether to repeat my objection so that Mr. Zupljanin knows what my objection is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My objection is to the following: That the -- that Mr. Cvijetic put to Judge Peric at line 20 -- sorry, page 20, line 2: "There was an initiative launched by the workers and colleagues from the judicial building. It was a petition asking for your resignation. Do you know that document?" "No," said Judge Peric, "that was in regard to the president of the court, not the public prosecutor. I had only two employees, and neither of them asked for me to be relieved of duty." And Mr. Cvijetic then put or said or made a statement: "You see, these are unofficial, informal acts, and the position of this Defence in regard to such documents and newspaper articles is such we do not consider them relevant evidence." And my objection is this: If it is not intended to put the document for whatever spurious reason before the witness or the Court, then the question should never have been asked in the first place. And there certainly should be no mention of newspaper articles and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, may I have clarification, Mr. Cvijetic, because my impression was the opposites of Ms. Korner, in that I thought you were eschewing the use of or reference to these articles. Is Ms. Korner's impression correct, that the foundation of your question to the witness is the basis of these articles, which you at the same time are saying shouldn't be relied on?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it wasn't interpreted properly, obviously. I did not base my question on any articles, nor did I refer to any articles. I presented the position of this Defence team. Namely, the position of this Defence team is that on the basis of such unofficial documents or, alternatively, newspaper articles - because we have a position on them as well - evidence could -- cannot be led before this Tribunal. I did not say that there were newspaper articles about Mr. Peric, I just presented our position, in principle, in relation to such indirect evidence. And then I decided to move to the official documents that I wanted to put to Mr. Peric. It was the witness who, in his statement, discussed such unofficial initiatives. In other words, my intention is to discuss here with Mr. Peric the official reasons for his dismissal, and I only asked him whether he was aware of such informal ones. He had mentioned them in his statement, but I will not be using them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I still don't -- I still don't -- Sorry. I still don't understand the connection then between the two points. He suggests, in terms, and if it wasn't a suggestion perhaps he would like to withdraw because that's the way I saw it, that Judge Peric was removed from his position as public prosecutor as a result of petitions that were placed before -- signed by his - I'm sorry, can I just go back again - initiative launched by workers and colleagues from the judicial building. "Do you know that document?" That was the thing. No, he says, that was something completely different. And then Mr. Cvijetic goes on to say these are unofficial, informal acts. Now, can -- maybe it's me and I'm not following this, but is the suggestion -- is the suggestion to Judge Peric is that there was such a petition? That's the first question. And is it suggested that this petition was reported in the newspapers? And that's what -- that's what Mr. Cvijetic is not relying on. But I think the most important thing is, Is that what the suggestion is? That he was removed as a result of this petition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, perhaps it would be less confusing if you were to not conflate these two things. And, as I understand the first part of your question, and Ms. Korner's understanding is the same as mine, deals with the -- there being some official basis and put -- leave aside this question of -- of newspaper articles because it only adds confusion to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That was what I wanted to do, and I've asked for document 1D03-3321 to be put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cvijetic, just deal with this, please. It's very simple. Are you suggesting to the judge that he was removed, whatever the official reasons were, because there was a petition? If so, can you put the question directly to him, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I first wanted to ask the witness whether he is aware of it because he mentions it in his statement. He answered that he didn't know of it, and I do have a document which shows the official reasons for his dismissal. And what I intend to do now is to deal with the official reasons. I will not be dealing with any petitions or any other reasons. I wanted to ask the witness whether he has heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, Your Honours, it is quite important. I know we're wasting quite a lot of time on what should be a simple point. Why does it matter whether he had heard of it or not if is not the Defence case that he was removed because of it? If it is the Defence case, that he was removed because of the petition, they must put that as a question. It is a simple, straightforward proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, I agree with Ms. Korner. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know for how many times do I have to ask for this document to be put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, we've found this document as part of the disclosed material. This is a -- these are minutes from an Assembly session, the session where your dismissal was discussed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you see, under 5, that Branko Peric should be --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read that part so that you would remember the events. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in the seventh and the eighth paragraph there in both versions. Yes, I think we them on the screen. So we have the reason for your dismissal set out; namely, it is claimed here that you have taken part in political activities, although you were a public prosecutor, by drafting some texts and so on. You mentioned that also when giving your statement. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what is it that it is stated here. This is in very general terms. I can make only conclusions and inferences. I did give an interview to a magazine from Belgrade, "Nin," where several texts were published in relation to legal issues, reasons for the rise of crime. I believe these were legal texts, such as materials that somebody who is an expert can freely write about. This was not being involved in politics. In the decision on my dismissal, there were no statement of reasons. I didn't know why I was dismissed, but I did see a letter from the SDS from Teslic that was sent to the Main Board which was the real organ of power. I have seen the request for my dismissal, and the reasons stated there were something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that for public prosecutors, people in the judicial organs, and judges, it was, so to speak, prohibited to act publicly in political sense and to present their political views?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that goes without saying. But I didn't do such things. My republican public prosecutor did not have any complaints. I've asked him whether he would put in a proposal for my dismissal. I do not see this as proper legal reasons. I do not see anything that would be a basis for a dismissal. This looks like a general position because it -- something needed to be put -- before the Assembly because they wanted to have me dismissed, and something had to be put before the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you would agree that the public prosecutor of the Republic agreed with this. We can see that in the text?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. One can see that. But the public prosecutor told me that Radovan Karadzic personally excerpted pressure asking him to request for my dismissal, that he had refused to do it on several occasion because I was very good prosecutor but told me that eventually he had to yield; he told me to come to Banja Luka and inform me that I will be dismissed during the next Assembly session. He said that Radovan had told him it's going to be either Peric going or you're going to be going.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I know, please, which Assembly -- we've only got one page. Could I know, please, which Assembly session this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The session held on the 14th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let me show you another official document, 1D03-3312.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the translation is pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you anticipated the question that I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is pending. And based on this information that was sent by MUP Republika Srpska Banja Luka, RDB Centre I will read only three lines and then Mr. Peric can confirm that we read it properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can I be told what tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, can you please confirm for me -- have you found the document, first of all, under tab 22?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that this is information issued by the Republika Srpska MUP State Security Centre Banja Luka, 6th of September 1994?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that from the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This information --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just before we go on. Firstly, where does this document come from? Because it's got no stamp, no seal, nothing to indicate what it is. It's a document that is - one, two, three, four - six pages long.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's part of the disclosure. It has its ERN number, and it's obvious that it's a document issued by the Republika Srpska MUP. We had no reason to doubt the authenticity of this document. Would that be okay then?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, this information deals with illegal activities by the person mentioned in the document who was a general manager of a company in Teslic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, it is stated that since the beginning of the war conflicts up until today his criminal actions blossomed. Can you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask for page 2, to be shown on the screen. And there's a piece of interesting information there. Can we please have page 2, the last paragraph, on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here your name is mentioned. Using your authority, you covered him in his illegal activities, his thievery, and that you received an apartment, five rooms, in return. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. Mr. Rade Pavlovic was a man who was not supporting the policies of the SDS. He openly fought against such policies. All the claims here about his criminal activities is untrue. The purpose of it was to discredit him and to dismiss him. He was a man with reputation, with authority, who was protecting his employees of Bosniak and Croat nationality. SDS did not like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested only is this bit related to you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must explain everything so that would you understand the situation. It is true that he donated an apartment with five rooms. It was owned by a Muslim, and this Muslim actually -- I was told at least that this worker of his who had died just before and whose wife and family would have inherited the apartment, and, in the meantime, I was supposed to make sure that nobody else moves, and did I that. I did receive the apartment from Rade Pavlovic, and I returned it back and gave it to the family immediately after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your curriculum vitae it is stated that after you were dismissed from the position of public prosecutor you started working as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the dismissal, I fled to Serbia because there was a mobilisation summons waiting for me already. I returned to Bosnia only after the Dayton Agreements. And after half a year of unemployment, I accepted a position in a news agency in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you the following document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 1D03-3323.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Tab 36 for you, sir, and for the Prosecutor. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, it is stated that this very general manager we discussed recently employed you after you were dismissed as the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Wait. Is this just a coincidence, or is that through certain -- because you did not inform us about working for him. You told us that you worked as a journalist only.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well this is general knowledge. That was the only man who dared to accept me as his employee. I don't think SDS would have taken me on. I worked there for only six months, if you allow --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My only question to you is, Why did you not tell us that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- you didn't ask me that question. I cannot answer the questions before you put them to me. I assume that you would want to ask me what you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But that's not stated in your curriculum vitae or your statement.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are so many things that are not there. I couldn't have put everything in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The problem is in the fact that the information issued by the MUP concerning the illegal activities of this gentleman you are mentioned as someone who was covering up for him, and here we see him protecting you and providing you employment, which is something that you did not inform us about, neither in your curriculum vitae, nor in the interviews.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never believed there was any need for that, and I wasn't covering up for anyone. If you have evidence to confirm that I was, please show them to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have only one more question and that will be my last question. And if I'm allowed, I would like to do it before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I just noticed that we are two minutes over the time for the break. But if your question is very, very short, admitting a very short answer, perhaps it would be more efficient to deal with it now. Or should we take the break, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I would like to complete my question. It will be a short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, the municipality of Teslic and the municipality of Doboj were subject to non-selective, to put it in that way, bombardment and artillery fire by Muslim and Croat sides, causing death to civilians as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I have information that between 10 and 15 civilians were casualties in Teslic; and in Doboj up to 50.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm for Teslic. I don't know about Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In Doboj -- I just apologise ... for Doboj I said there were more than 90. I would like to make a correction to the transcript. Not 50, but more than 90. There is a monument for the casualties. Can you confirm whether you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... other than -- before the judge answers and before we take the break, other than the Defence are tu quoque, which is not a defence, what issue -- or what is the relevance or this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be convenient to take the break at this point. We will return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours I would like to make a correction to the numbering given to the 92 ter package yesterday. 65 ter number 10359.01 is issued exhibit number P01361.01. 65 ter number 10359.02 is issued exhibit number P1361.02. 65 ter 09045 is issued exhibit number 1361.03. 65 ter 10359.03 is issued exhibit number P01361.04. 65 ter 00870 is issued exhibit number P01361.05. And finally, 65 ter 02758 is issued exhibit number P01361.06. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we reconnect with the witness, I would just like to tender two documents that I've shown to the witness. This decision on his appointment an employment, he identified it as the decision, on the basis of which he worked. It's 1D03-3323. And I kindly ask you to decide on its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. At this time I rise to my feet. I'm not sure what document Mr. Cvijetic is referring to. Is it the one about his employment in 1996? And the relevance of that would be to any issue in this case, I ask? That was a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I understood Mr. Cvijetic's line of questions to be, because you would recall that I intervened on several occasions, what I believe I understood the purpose of that to be is that the exigencies of the wartime situation as obtained meant there were any number of anomalies or irregularities. One of them being the way in which the witness was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I think we may be at cross purposes. I think he is trying to put in - and that's why I'm trying to check - the one where he got the job with the company. I don't think -- I have no objection to -- I don't think that -- I may already -- I have no objection to the one where he is appointed prosecutor, but I think he is trying to put in the one where he was appointed as the legal advisor to this company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... 1996?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's why I'm asking what on earth the relevance is to anything in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... from his CV, and I assume it went to credibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honour, that's fine. He's being asked about it, you've got the answers. I can't see that this is a document that Your Honours are going to be pouring over at the end of this case. And, Your Honour, I'm simply taking the view that if Your Honours want to limit documents to what is strictly relevant, then how on earth - the fact that he missed out from his CV and he's given explanation - needs the document in to show that he was appointed as the legal advisor to a company?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, what is your response to that? We have the evidence. Do we need the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I put those questions precisely for the purpose which you just stated. Your understanding is correct. The witness claimed that he had been forced to flee Republika Srpska for the reasons he had stated. However, these claims are not true because he found employment with a company whose manager is claimed to have been involved in illegal activities. Since in his testimony and in his statement the witness holds himself out to be a man of the law, my examination followed the course that you had seen. And the document I tendered a moment ago goes to the punch line of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose it does have utility in that it, as it were, ties up this line of inquiry. So where as it probably strictly is unnecessary because we have the evidence, it should be admitted as an exhibit in my view and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document ID 03-3323 is given Exhibit 1D276. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And there was second document, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the document before, from the National Security Service, Banja Luka, which points out the illegal activities of the general manager concerned and the reward given to this witness while he was a prosecutor. The witness has explained under what circumstances he received that apartment and what happened with it. And although I'm not sure that this document currently meets the standard for admission, I suggest it be MFI'd. And we will then try to tender it when we have a witness from the National Security Service. And it is also awaiting a translation. That's another reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... going to suggest that it be marked for identification because inasmuch as it is awaiting translation, the Prosecution, once they would have had an opportunity to consider the English version and seen the context of the excerpt that you put to the witness, may have a view on it. So at this point we just mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to say that. Your Honour, I'm slightly unhappy that a document that a witness who's been known to be coming for weeks now and a document which the Defence consider important and runs to six pages has not been translated and it's sought to put part of it in. I'm hoping that we can organise a translation - I don't know how much longer Mr. Cvijetic or Mr. Krgovic have - but I'm hoping that we can organise a translation, which I would have though they could have done, at some speed so we can see what this document is actually all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So for the moment it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document ID 03-3312 is exhibited as 1D277, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question about this shelling and casualties among civilians is simple and it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to this question. I repeat the objection. To what issue, other than an attempt to put tu quoque forward as a defence, do these questions about shelling by Croats and/or Muslims in areas of Doboj or Teslic and memorials to the fallen heros go? What is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness was not a simple citizen. He is a qualified prosecutor, authorised to start investigations and criminal proceedings in war crimes cases. My question to him is straightforward: Did those who ordered and perpetrated this shelling become indicted and tried in this BH Court, which is still trying perpetrators of such crimes? Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask that question in relation to Teslic. He cannot ask it in relation to Doboj or anywhere else or Tesanj in which Judge Peric was not the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree. Let the witness answer, and that will complete my examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the perpetrators of the shelling have been tried. As far as I know, the shells came from the Tesnjak [as interpreted] area, but that also is my indirect knowledge. I don't know whether this was prosecuted. I know that the police explained to me that evidence is being prepared for this for a state authority that would deal with war crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Peric, thank you for your testimony. I have no further questions for you. Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Peric. I am Dragan Krgovic appearing for Stojan Zupljanin's Defence. I will question you about the events that you discussed with the Prosecutor and with Mr. Cvijetic over the past few days. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We speak the same language and we should try not to overlap and not to speak too fast. I am saying this to myself as well. And we are less -- we are more familiar with these events than the interpreters are, so let's try to avoid overlapping. I'd like to deal with one topic you spoke about, and I need some clarification. When you were replying to the Prosecutor and to Mr. Cvijetic earlier today, you mentioned the exhumation and possible post mortem for Muslims and Croats who had been killed. You said, if I understood well, that the issue of exhumations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we have just temporarily lost the link with Sarajevo. Could you just hold on for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand that the video is back. They're waiting for the audio to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps you should begin your preliminary remarks again, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Peric, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just repeat. Responding to the questions of the Prosecutor and Mr. Cvijetic, you mentioned exhumations. I'd like a clarification. Under the prevailing legislation and practice at the time, exhumation and post mortems were investigative steps taken normally by the investigating judge with the help of the experts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, following an application by the authorised prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it is the investigating judge who issues a decision, ordering these investigative steps to be taken?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And from what I remember of the criminal procedure and practice, those are the only two investigative steps that the investigating judge and the prosecutor may not entrust to the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because the investigating judge or the prosecutor may order the police to take certain investigating step, such as collecting information, securing the crime scene, et cetera, something that falls within the remit of the police; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the police, apart from securing the crime scene upon the order of the investigating judge, has nothing to do with exhumation and post mortems?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But they would probably be present, securing the site of exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant. Exclusively at the request of the investigating judge, they would be called in to secure the site.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And could you assist me with one more thing. My colleague, Mr. Cvijetic, showed you the Law on Criminal Procedure, and I'll show you an article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P120.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's your tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court Article 45. In B/C/S, it's page 51; and English, page 14.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me the number of the article?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As I understand this Article 45, item(1) in paragraph (2), the prosecutor has a certain role to play in pre-indictment proceedings.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He may have a role in pre-indictment proceedings, in issuing certain instructions to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the normal practice was, at least in peacetime, that before a criminal report is submitted, the police could come for a consultation with the prosecutor to see how to qualify a certain act and how to take certain steps.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in your evidence you spoke about your travel to Banja Luka and the meetings you had in Banja Luka. You met with those people you mentioned, Mr. Stevilovic, Mr. Markovic, Mr. Perisic, and Mr. Zupljanin in the office of Mr. Zupljanin at the CSB Banja Luka, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And one of the topics I'd like to remind you and one of the reasons for your presence there, apart from the reasons you mentioned, was the discussion that if the police submit a criminal report against this Mice Group, they're remanned in custody and further prosecution needed to be ensured.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In line with Article 45 of this law, paragraph 2.1, suggestions needed to be made for this entire undertaking to be successful.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there was discussion about that. I really can't recall the details, but I suppose we discussed that, among other things, how to complete that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that chief of the police do their job, if they arrest the perpetrators and turn them over to the investigating judge and the prosecutor to be remanded in custody. The whole operation would be pointless.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That went without saying, that these people would be remanded in custody and placed under guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was one of the purposes of that meeting you attended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, of course, that was the reason why the prosecutor and the president of the high court in Banja Luka were present?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I'm coming to this conclusion; namely, the idea was to have this measure of detention to be taken in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you returned to Teslic on the very same day. And on the evening of that day, or maybe the following day, the arrest took place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume we returned on the same day. I'm not sure whether the arrest took place on the next day, or maybe in a day or two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will skip some events. And once the Doboj High Court requested for the persons to be transferred from Banja Luka to Doboj, that was something that's under the jurisdiction of judicial organs exclusively; this has nothing to do with police activities. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that has nothing to do with the police. I think that was done along the line president of the court and the prison. The police had no authorities in relation to detention. None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Especially in a case when the investigative judge has issued a measure of detention and when these people are in detention under the control of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment. I just need to check in the transcript whether your answer was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. What my colleague tells me is that since my question was that the detention unit was immediately under the control of the higher court and the Ministry of Justice, so I would like to ask you to confirm whether you agree that both of these organs keep control over that institution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let us go back to a part of your answer in response to a question put to you by Ms. Korner concerning work obligation. I -- do you remember that you were interviewed -- and this document is part of the evidence. It was in December of 2001 and January 2002 that you gave an interview to the OTP. And, of course, your recollection was much better at the time, since nine years have elapsed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me read to you a question and an answer that are related to my intervention made yesterday. Pages 28 and 29 of the transcript. I'll read in English, and you'll hear it interpreted. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... if the work obligations also included digging trenches on the front line? [Interpretation] And your answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So sorry. Pages 28 and 29 of which interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: 28 and 29 -- interview -- [Interpretation] It's 2002 interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that 28 and 29 in a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not have the translation of it. I'm reading from the English version. [In English] If you want to check, because that's the only copy I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm so sorry, Your Honours, but I'm looking at page 28 and 29 of the English version of the interview in 2002, and this is about civilian protection. Oh, I see. Yep. Got it. Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We do not have a B/C/S version of this interview. What we did was we were trying to establish the same -- to be on the same page, us and the Prosecutor, so -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... in the war it included the digging of the trenches. And when you say later, on what time-frame is that approximately? [Interpretation] You responded: [In English] [Previous translation continues] "... 1994 when the activities were already under way when the separation line between the two armies had already been formed." [Interpretation] I conclude from this that when you spoke about work obligation you spoke in general terms; and when the Prosecutor asked when these people were going to dig trenches, you referred to 1993 and 1994. Do you remember whether that was what you told them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I cannot give you a precise time. I cannot remember these events with any certainty. It may have been in 1992. But it was certainly at the time when the lines were being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in 2001, you said 1993 and 1994. I assume your recollection of the events was better at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were also talking about armament of citizens of Muslim ethnicity, and you mentioned that you had heard rumours about that. Did you hear that weapons for some Croat and Muslim formations in that border area, bordering with Tesanj, that they were received from the municipality of Tesanj, that they were armed by the municipality of Tesanj? Did you hear stories to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I cannot make any comments, any specific comments. I do know that there were rumours, but I think it was more of an individually based sale of weapons. Individual Serbs were selling weapons to Muslims. I think the price that I've heard of was about 1.000 German marks per piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, yesterday, when you were talking about military operations in Stenjak and Rankovici, as far as I understood, you are not familiar with the details related to the operation itself, what caused it, what was the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not that with any degree of certainty. I know that this was a joint operation by military and the police. I remember the operation related to Stenjak. The court building is about 500 metres from Stenjak, and I do remember seeing a tank placed on a bridge. That's the only part I have seen first-hand. I know that after that, the village was emptied of inhabitants. There were no more Muslims in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the conflict started when a Muslim unit from Tesanj attacked a military patrol in Stenjak and that that was the cause of the conflict? Do you remember stories about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that two or three persons were arrested. I knew one of them personally. I think his name was Boro Dojkovic. And that there were negotiations concerning their exchange, or rather, about having them back. That I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. There was this officer by the name of Dojkovic; he was arrested, together with two of his soldiers, and he was taken to Tesanj. This group took him there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but I don't know whether that was the immediate cause of the conflict, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you also know that -- maybe you have heard, namely, that a military police patrol was attacked that came to intervene and that several people were wounded in the ambush operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Stenjak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some talks about the patrol, but I don't know any details concerning those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the villages were emptied of its inhabitants. What you're saying here -- or, rather, you're only talking about the consequences.
